Empirical Research Plan – “Does Trade Raise Living Standards?”  
(One–year, cross-country study, 1985)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy chosen: Cross-sectional Two-Stage Least Squares (Instrumental-Variables).

Rationale  
•  The outcome (real income per person in 1985) and the treatment (openness = exports + imports divided by GDP, 1985) are both observed only once; DID/event-study designs are infeasible.  
•  Openness is plausibly endogenous (rich countries trade more; trade policy responds to income); an instrument is therefore required.  
•  Geography—distances to partners, land-area, common borders, landlocked status—is predetermined, plausibly exogenous to 1985 income, and powerfully predicts bilateral trade through the gravity equation.  
•  Aggregating the gravity-predicted bilateral flows yields a country-level “predicted trade share” that varies strongly across countries but does not respond to contemporary economic or policy shocks.  

Hence a gravity-based IV is the natural design.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable  
Ti  = actual trade share of country i in 1985 = (Xi + Mi)/GDPi.

Instrument (quasi-experimental variation)  
Ťi  = predicted trade share for country i obtained in two steps:  
 1. Estimate gravity:   
  ln(Tradeij) = α + β1 ln(Distanceij) + β2 Borderij + β3 Landlockedi + β4 Landlockedj  
       + β5 (ln Areai + ln Areaj) + εij,   using bilateral flows 1985.  
 2. Set Tradeij at its fitted value from the above, sum j≠i, divide by GDPi.  

Control group / counterfactual  
Countries whose geographic characteristics predict low trade exposure provide the counterfactual for otherwise-similar countries with high predicted exposure. There is no explicit time or running variable.

Extension (within-country trade)  
Di  = ln(Populationi) is added to the structural equation; because population may itself be endogenous, we instrument it with ln (Area)i, exploiting that a bigger land mass raises the scope for internal trade but is predetermined.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Relevance – Geography strongly predicts openness  
 • F-stat on Ťi in the first stage comfortably > 10.  
 • Highly plausible (gravity evidence for centuries).

A2. Exclusion – Geography affects 1985 income only through trade (and population, if used as second endogenous regressor).  
 • Plausibility: distance to foreign markets, borders, landlockedness matter primarily through trade costs.  
 • Concerns: Geography may influence income through climate, natural resources, disease environment, or tourism.

A3. Independence – Geographical characteristics are predetermined and not chosen in response to 20th-century income shocks.  
 • Highly plausible; countries cannot change physical location or borders easily (aside from rare partitions).

A4. No general-equilibrium spillovers that violate SUTVA  
 • A single country’s geography-driven trade change does not materially affect world prices/income.

A5. Linear constant-elasticity functional form correctly approximates the trade–income relationship.  
 • Testable using flexible controls and log-log robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations

T1. Omitted geographic variables that influence productivity directly (e.g., tropical disease burden).  
  Mitigation: Control for latitude, malaria ecology, oil-exporter dummy, terrain ruggedness; check robustness to including those variables.

T2. Institutional quality correlated with both geography and income (e.g., European settlement pattern theory).  
  Mitigation: Add rule-of-law or ex-colonizer fixed effects; re-estimate on sub-samples with similar colonial history; use over-identification tests (distance vs. landlocked vs. borders only).

T3. Measurement error / zero-trade pairs dropped.  
  Mitigation: Use Poisson-pseudo-ML gravity (which allows zeros); aggregate fitted bilateral flows using all country pairs; winsorize extreme trade/GDP ratios.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  (executability assumes three CSVs in working directory)

```r
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast lm, iv
library(sandwich)    # robust vcov
library(lmtest)      # coeftest

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
bilat <- read_csv("bilateral_trade_1985.csv")     # i, j, trade_ij
macro  <- read_csv("pennworld_1985.csv")          # country, rgdppc, trade_share, pop, gdp
geo    <- read_csv("geography_vars.csv")          # country, area, landlocked, lat, ...

# 2. Gravity first stage ---------------------------------------------------
bilat2 <- bilat %>%
  left_join(select(geo, country=i, area_i=area, landlocked_i=landlocked),
            by=c("i"="country")) %>%
  left_join(select(geo, country=j, area_j=area, landlocked_j=landlocked),
            by=c("j"="country"))

grav_eq <- feols(log(trade_ij) ~ log(distance) + border +
                   landlocked_i + landlocked_j +
                   log(area_i) + log(area_j),
                 data = bilat2)
bilat2$log_trade_hat <- predict(grav_eq)

# 3. Construct predicted openness -----------------------------------------
pred_open <- bilat2 %>%
  mutate(trade_hat = exp(log_trade_hat)) %>%
  group_by(i) %>%
  summarise(pred_trade = sum(trade_hat)) %>%
  rename(country = i)

macro <- macro %>%
  left_join(pred_open, by = "country") %>%
  left_join(geo,  by = "country") %>%
  mutate(open_hat = pred_trade / gdp,
         ln_income = log(rgdppc),
         ln_open   = log(trade_share),
         ln_open_hat = log(open_hat),
         ln_pop  = log(pop),
         ln_area = log(area))

# 4. Two-stage least squares ----------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(ln_income ~ 1 | ln_open ~ ln_open_hat , data = macro,
                 vcov = ~continent)          # cluster on continents optional
summary(iv_main)

# 5. Extended: joint IV for openness & population -------------------------
iv_two <- feols(ln_income ~ 1 | ln_open + ln_pop ~ ln_open_hat + ln_area,
                data = macro, vcov = ~continent)
summary(iv_two)

# 6. Robustness: add latitude, oil dummy ----------------------------------
iv_rob <- feols(ln_income ~ latitude + oil_exporter |
                  ln_open ~ ln_open_hat , data = macro,
                vcov = ~continent)
summary(iv_rob)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results

Theory (standard gains-from-trade models) predicts a positive elasticity:
β ≡ d ln (Y/N) / d ln (Trade/GDP)  > 0.

Calibrations with Armington or Melitz models suggest β ≈ 0.2–0.3 under reasonable trade cost reductions. An openness difference of one standard deviation (~30 pp of GDP) should translate into ≈6–8 percent higher real income per person.

For population (internal market size), models with increasing returns suggest a smaller but still positive elasticity, perhaps 0.05–0.10.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)

C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10) ...................... 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction (geography ↛ income except via trade).. 0.5  
C3: Independence / as-good-as-random assignment of instrument .... 1  
C4: No interference across units (SUTVA) ........................ 0.5  
C5: Correct functional specification / monotonicity ............. 0.5  
Total (out of 5) = 3.5  → Acceptable but not perfect; sensitivity analyses essential.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers a transparent, gravity-based IV estimate of the causal effect of openness (and, secondarily, domestic market size) on living standards, addresses the main threats, and is feasible with the specified data.
